# Timeline, station and map sources

Research register assembled **23 September 2026** for the eight systems then in the repository; the Chengdu, Beijing, Nanjing and Chongqing sections were added on **24 September 2026** from new research, the Seoul section on **25 September 2026**, and the Xi'an section on **27 September 2026**. Later corrections are dated where they are described. The final audits of **3 October 2026** rechecked every system's events, stations, tracks and geography through 2 October 2026.

This file preserves references recovered from earlier research and adds newly located corroboration. For the first twelve systems and Xi'an it indexes **every current event entry and every legend line**, including historical predecessors, trams, light rail and gondolas; the Seoul section summarises its sources by topic instead. It also records sources for station/transfer identities, kilometres, drawn geography and logos.

The Tokyo, Shenzhen, Hangzhou and Guangzhou line-history references were largely recovered from earlier map-building research. Most Hong Kong, Shanghai, Taipei, Singapore and Foshan line-history links were located again for this register; they should not be represented as a recovered original bibliography. The existing spec also preserved several original Hong Kong and geographic references.

**Coverage is not the same as verification.** Some entries still have only a secondary chronology, some exact days are placeholders, and some historical distances/coordinates are estimates. Those limitations are recorded below; this is not a claim that every existing value has a reliable primary citation. No timeline data or geometry was changed while assembling this register.

## How to read and maintain this file

- **Recovered** means the reference was found in the existing spec, earlier research files or their bibliographies. It does not mean the original author of every asset can be proven to have used it.
- **New** means a reference located for this register; it corroborates existing data rather than proving its original provenance.
- **Recovered citation** links preserve useful original notices and contemporary reports cited by the earlier research. They have not all been independently reopened; a link is not a claim of successful retrieval. Archives and WeChat in particular may block automated access.
- **Secondary chronology** means a line/station history, usually Wikipedia. It is useful for locating dated primary evidence, but must not settle a disputed day merely because the repo agrees with it.
- **Unresolved / unverified day** identifies a specific claim that still needs evidence. A source for a line opening does not automatically substantiate a rename, delayed station or paid-area change listed in the same event.
- Event-table descriptions below are an inventory copied from the repository, **not quotations from the linked sources**. Sources apply only to their stated subject. The table deliberately preserves questionable entries so they can be corrected in the data after verification.
- **Station markers.** Bullets dated before 2026-10-01 that mention capsules, pills or capsule axes describe the earlier marker model. Each system's 2026-10-01 "Station markers" bullet describes platform points and bridges, and its "Interchange shapes (2026-10-01)" bullet which platforms are drawn as one shape (spec §5); where they differ, the interchange shapes bullet is current, as amended by the later close-platforms (0.4 R) and final audit bullets.
- **Tracks.** Bullets dated before 2026-10-03 that describe corridors 3.5–5 units or `2 W` apart, tracks widened or bent to clear or reach a marker, or a 12° smoothness limit describe the earlier track rules. Each system's "Final audit (2026-10-03)" bullets describe the current geometry (spec §4); where they differ, they are current.
- Prefer operator notices and dated maps; then government records, contemporary reporting and scholarly histories; then secondary timelines and their footnotes. A planned opening, trial without public passengers, construction completion or ceremony is not necessarily first passenger service.

### What needs a source

| Stored fact                                                       | Evidence to use                                                                                                                             |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `events.json`: each date and each description                     | Event index below; resolve each independent claim, not just the first description on the date.                                              |
| `lines.json`: historical names and start/end dates                | Line histories and dated naming notices; corporate establishment, service takeover and public renaming can occur on different days.         |
| SVG track labels: opening, removal, reassignment                  | Opening/withdrawal notices and historical route diagrams; end dates are exclusive, so first absent day may be the day after last operation. |
| SVG station labels: name, opening, relocation, marker replacement | Line station tables plus station-specific histories and operator plans; a marker upgrade is not a newly opened physical station.            |
| SVG `data-lines`, connectors and station identity                 | Dated interchange diagrams and fare-area notices. Walking connection, continuous fare and shared paid area are different facts.             |
| SVG `data-km`                                                     | Published operating section length, with rounding/allocation documented; not the length of the Bézier path.                                 |
| SVG route/station/water coordinates                               | Original map provenance, engineering alignment and mapped geographic features; modern geometry does not establish historical geometry.      |
| Colours, logos and compact interchange shapes                     | Operator wayfinding/map and original artwork. These are presentation choices, not extra historical events.                                  |

The date boundaries in the indexed `map.svg` files (station/track labels and `data-lines`) and their `lines.json` legends were compared with their `events.json`: **none fall on a date absent from the event index**. This checks coverage of dates, not correctness or completeness of every description. Source links for the line station tables also cover intermediate stations omitted from event prose.

Use [the map data spec](map-data-spec.md#11-sources-and-verification) for scope and parsing. This is a build history: maintenance, accidents and temporary operating suspensions normally do not erase built track. Lines are drawn exactly when the public could ride them, including public previews, free trial rides, experience weeks, voucher rides, sightseeing, trial and restricted-access service (spec §7). When a preview came before the opening, both are events: the preview names its kind of service, the line is drawn from its first public rides onward with no gap and no "rides end" event, and the opening is recorded as its own event even when it changes nothing on the map. A preview followed by more than a year without service is left off the map; the line then appears at its regular opening. Test runs without passengers, ceremonies and VIP rides, and open days without rides are noted but not drawn.

## Accuracy gaps to keep visible

1. **Hong Kong:** 1913 Sheung Shui halt and other early KCR/Sha Tau Kok halts are not fully inventoried; Hung Hom 1921 closure and 1996 names need exact-day evidence (Kowloon Tong's 1982-05-04 opening now rests on a contemporary newspaper cited in the event index). Several 1960s rename dates encode only a known year. Historical KCR geometry and Light Rail stage lengths are estimates. Under the spec §7 rule the MTR's 1979-09-30 open day, Light Rail's free rides (1988-09-14–16), West Rail's charity trial days (2003-12-16–18), the East Tsim Sha Tsui extension's one-day trial (2004-10-17, zh-wiki only) and Ma On Shan Rail's charity ride day (2004-12-19) are drawn from their first public day and stay on the map; each opening (1979-10-01, 1988-09-18, 2003-12-20, 2004-10-24, 2004-12-21) is its own event. The Airport Railway's 1998-06-12 public open day is not drawn because it is not known whether trains were ridden.
2. **Shanghai:** early surface-alignment replacements, paid-area passage dates and exact English naming rollouts need stronger primary evidence. The English timeline and other histories disagree on the first Line 3 day. Under the spec §7 rule Line 2 appears on 1999-09-20 (organised visits, then sightseeing; regular service 2000-06-11), the Expo Line on 2010-04-20 (invited-visitor trial days; all Expo visitors from 2010-05-01) and Songjiang Tram 2 on 2018-12-20 (free trial rides, continuing into its 2018-12-26 opening), each later step with its own event; the October 1999 start of public Line 2 sightseeing has no exact day. Two openings may be earlier than recorded but keep their dates because the first public day is not established: Line 1's southern section (1993-05-28) had one-train sightseeing from 28 January or 9 April 1993 (sources disagree, continuity unknown); its Xujiahui – Shanghai Railway Station section (1995-04-10) reportedly had sightseeing from 28 December 1994 (secondary sources only); the Maglev's 2003 sightseeing pause (2003-03-10 – 09-19, from its published timetable and the 2004 yearbook) is not drawn. Line 8's 16 September 2007 non-stop ride for 260 invited residents at a Transport Week ceremony is not counted. Line 22 (testing since 2026-08-26) and the Line 13 extensions had not opened by 2026-10-02 and are not drawn.
3. **Taipei:** extension dates do not by themselves prove when modern combined line names became official. Some stored section kilometres differ from operator historical tables. Muzha (1996-02-27), the Tucheng extension (2006-05-27, Banqiao–Tucheng, one day), the Neihu section (2009-06-29 – 07-01), the Airport MRT (2017-02-16) and the Circular Line (2020-01-19) appear with their free public trial rides, and their openings (1996-03-28, 2006-05-31, 2009-07-04, 2017-03-02, 2020-01-31) are separate events (spec §7). The Xiaobitan branch's 24 September 2004 free trial ride is uncited and not used. The Xinyi Line eastern extension (Xiangshan – Guangci/Fengtian Temple) opened on 2026-08-30 without a public preview; the new station's position is projected from OpenStreetMap through the existing fit, and the Tamsui–Xinyi Line's 31.1 km adds the published 1.4 km to the stored 29.7 km rather than a published line total. Labels use current Hanyu Pinyin names throughout, although the operator used Wade-Giles names until 2003 and Danshui from 2003 to 2011.
4. **Singapore:** since 2009 most new stages had a one-day open house or public preview with free rides a few days to three weeks before regular service; each is drawn from that day onwards, with no gap before regular service, and followed by an opening event (spec §7). The 2009 Circle Line open house (23 May, Bartley–Marymount) and the 13 January 2012 Circle Line extension open house are attested as having free rides only by a blog and keep their regular dates; the NEL 2003 preview lead and pre-2009 open days are unconfirmed (the 1987–1990 open days were station viewings without trains). Early East–West naming and exact section kilometres need checking beyond a current network map. The Downtown Line extension (Xilin, Sungei Bedok) and Thomson–East Coast Line Stage 5 had not opened by 2026-10-02; add them, with any public preview, when they open.
5. **Tokyo:** Asakusa's out-of-station interchange is dated from the 1960-12-04 opening, although through ticketing began on 1961-06-01; Shibuya's Ginza–Hanzomon transfer (1978) and the New Line Ikebukuro transfer (1994) may have been in-gate. Eidan's corporate rename to Tokyo Metro (2004) is not modelled. The Akabane tram branch's 3.7 km is its drawn length at the tram's scale (no published section length was found), and the Toden and Liner stops are simplified (spec §8).
6. **Shenzhen:** SIAT → SUAT (2025-01-01) is a placeholder day: the operator updated its maps after May 2024 without a date, and the station's own signs changed only in January 2026. English station names on Lines 1 and 4 were pinyin until 2010–11, with no known switch date; the translated names are shown throughout. Unpaid passages that the operator does not list as transfers (Grand Theater – Hongling South, Dongmen – Laojie) have no connector. Simplified tram/Skyshuttle interchange markers deliberately compress real walking distances.
7. **Hangzhou:** October 2019 English Yuhang rename is month-only. Airport/railway-station continuous fares must not be mistaken for physically joined paid areas. Lines 1 and 2 appear with their free trial rides (2012-11-18 – 21 and 2014-11-18 – 22), stay on the map through regular service on 24 November, and that opening is its own event; which Line 1 stations the 2012 rides served is inferred from the opening arrangement.
8. **Guangzhou/Foshan:** May/November 2006 and September 2021 naming rollouts lack exact days. Under the spec §7 rule Line 1 appears with its paid sightseeing services (Xilang–Huangsha 1997-06-28, Huangsha–Guangzhou East 1999-02-16); the line then closed for final testing from 1999-03-03 until regular service on 1999-06-28, a pause the map does not draw (spec §7), so Line 1 stays on the map from 1997. When the 1997 sightseeing on Xilang–Huangsha ended (possibly by January 1999) is not established. The Guangfo Line appears with its trial rides (2010-10-28 – 29) and stays through its 2010-11-03 opening. Huangpu Tram 2's preview (2020-12-29 – 2021-01-03) was followed by over four years without service, so it is left off and the section appears at its 2025-06-20 opening. Line 12 length definitions differ between sources. Line 12's middle section and Line 13 phase 2 west were in operational testing on 2026-10-02 and are not drawn, and Line 11's Guangzhou Railway Station platform is still bypassed.
9. **Chengdu:** the July 2023 English renaming batch, the Jincheng Plaza English forms and the 2020 Chengdu Academy of Governance rename lack exact days (latest attested days are used). Line 2's east section was cut back from 2025-12-20 and returned on 2026-09-28 on its rebuilt alignment ([川观新闻](https://cbgc.scol.com.cn/news/7991007)). The new Longquanyi Railway Station between Chengdu Academy of Governance and Damianpu was not part of the reopening; it and the other built but unopened stations (Bairendian on Line 27, Yuhong Road and Fenshui on Line 30, the Line 10 platforms at People's Park and Wenweng Shishi, Lujia on S3) are added when they open. Line 8 phase 2, Line 10 phase 3 and several phase lengths are allocated from published totals. Lines 1 and 2 appear with their free trial rides (2010-09-10 – 12, 2012-09-01 – 03), stay on the map through their openings (2010-09-27, 2012-09-16), which are separate events; Line 1's trial dates rest on the zh-wiki chronology.
10. **Beijing:** Line 1 appears on 1971-01-15 and the Olympic branch on 2008-07-19 with restricted-access service (spec §7); their openings to all passengers (1972-12-27, 2008-10-09) and Line 1's formal opening (1981-09-15) are separate events. Exact days for Lixin/Gongzhufen, Bajiaocun/Bajiao Amusement Park, Xinhua Jie/Heping Men and Gucheng Lu/Gucheng renames remain unresolved. Those markers use current names; the map does not claim a complete day-resolved rename history. Historical Xi’erqi placement and section kilometres remain approximate. See the Beijing section for decisions and scope. Pingguoyuan (Line 1, 2020-04-18 → 2026-05-16) and Bajiao Amusement Park (from 2025-06-02) are drawn closed during their rebuilds; three-month works closures are not drawn. Line 22, in trial operation without passengers since 2026-08-25, is not drawn.
11. **Nanjing, Chongqing and Seoul:** their remaining evidence gaps are listed in their own sections (Nanjing's 2005 sightseeing extensions and subtitle renames; Chongqing's Xiejiawan (2005, display bound) and Zengjiayan (2005-06-15, zh-wiki only) opening days and rename rollouts; Seoul's undated romanization and subtitle changes). Chongqing's Line 15 (Jingkou – Liangjiang Film City) had its fares published from a tentative 1 October 2026, but no passenger opening was confirmed by 2 October, so it stays off the map. Seoul's GTX-A safety inspection by about 300 recruited citizens (19–22 March 2024, days unknown) and reported Shinbundang free rides (October 2011, fan wiki only) are not drawn.
12. **Xi'an:** the 2025 rename day (2025-12-22, first reported signage; zh.wikipedia says 2025-12-29), the paid-area status of 双寨's Line 3/14 transfer, the English names used on the Airport Intercity in 2019–21 and the undated numbered-road spelling change (`5-LU` → `5 LU`) remain open; see [its section](#xian). Line 1's 2013 trial-ride ticket distribution is inferred from its scale.
13. **Across systems:** a published present-day total does not prove each historical `data-km` allocation, and a geographic SVG is not a survey. Original artwork provenance remains incompletely recovered for several older systems. Under the spacing of separate stations close together (spec §5, an open decision), some circles stand off their platforms: out-of-station staggers of up to about 14 units (Shenzhen's Futian Checkpoint and Hongling South, Guangzhou's Linhexi, Canton Tower, Pazhou and Wuyangcun, Chengdu's Shuangliu Terminals 1 and 2, Tokyo's Ueno-hirokoji, Awajicho and Shibuya, Beijing's Sihui and Dazhong Si, Nanjing's Zhushanlu, Seoul's Noryangjin, Singapore's Newton) and the no-transfer spacing of Xi'an's Mutasixi (210 m) and Chongqing's Fotuguan. One documented track spacing also leaves a line off its course (spec §4): Hong Kong's Airport Express convention (the Tung Chung line up to 1.6 W off on Lantau and east of Tsing Yi).

<a id="hongkong"></a>

## Hong Kong — MTR / KCR (`hongkong`)

Assets: [events](../src/assets/hongkong/data/events.json), [line names](../src/assets/hongkong/data/lines.json), [SVG](../src/assets/hongkong/map.svg).

Scope follows the MTR network map, which includes the High Speed Rail's Hong Kong section and Light Rail (drawn as tracks only), plus the operator's own Ngong Ping 360 (spec §8). KCR lines are the predecessors of today's East Rail, Tuen Ma and Light Rail. Station tooltips show `kcr` until the 2007-12-02 merger and `mtr` from then on (spec §5); the merger's event is that day's renames.

### Primary records and other focused references

- [KCRC: history][p-mtr-kcrc] — **New**. Operator chronology, KCR opening, 1913 Sheung Shui halt, electrification, Light Rail and later projects; distinguish ceremonies from first passenger operation.
- [KCR annual report 1921, paragraph 19][p-mtr-1921] — **Recovered**. Original government report, hosted by Histsyn; Hung Hom / Ho Man Tin halt evidence. Does not settle the repo's exact Hung Hom closure day.
- [KCR annual report 1935, paragraphs 59 and 102][p-mtr-1935] — **Recovered**. Che Kung Miu experimental halt, 16 November 1935; location at Bridge 12.
- [KCR annual report 1936, paragraph 41][p-mtr-1936] — **Recovered**. Che Kung Miu withdrawal, 1 October 1936.
- [KCR annual report 1976][p-mtr-1976] — **Recovered**. 1975 Kowloon terminal relocation and historical route context.
- [Hong Kong Railway Museum: Fanling–Sha Tau Kok Branch][p-mtr-stk-museum] — **Recovered**. Museum account and historical alignment/station illustrations; stronger provenance than a modern inferred route.
- [R. J. Phillips: Sha Tau Kok Branch, a study 1911–1928][p-mtr-stk-study] — **New**. Historical study, not an operator notice; consult its primary citations for partial opening and closure dates.
- [Contemporary Light Rail opening notice (newspaper scan)][p-mtr-lr-preview] — **Recovered**. 14–16 September 1988 free public rides (drawn as a preview), no service on the 17th, fare-paying regular service from 18 September (the opening). Forum hosts the scan; the source is the newspaper notice.
- [Government daily information bulletin, 6 November 1991][p-mtr-lr-1991] — **Recovered**. Reports the extension opening on the preceding Sunday, 3 November; not 17 November.
- [LegCo: commissioning new railways, December 2003][p-mtr-lr-2003] — **Recovered**. Light Rail extensions opened 7 December; West Rail commissioning context.
- [MTR annual report 2018, Hong Kong transport operations][p-mtr-xrl-2018] — **Recovered**. Hong Kong high-speed rail opening, 23 September 2018.
- [MTR business overview][p-mtr-km] — **Recovered**. Published route lengths; Hong Kong XRL 25.7 km versus rounded 26 km project descriptions. Current totals do not certify every historical section allocation.
- [LegCo: XRL project report and alignment, December 2016][p-mtr-xrl-plan] — **Recovered**. Engineering alignment; Hong Kong section extent. The drawn continuation into Shenzhen is context, not additional Hong Kong kilometres.
- [MTR corporate profile][p-mtr-merger] — **New**. Rail merger on 2 December 2007; operator identity context for KCR/MTR labels.
- [MTR annual reports and results archive][p-mtr-reports] — **New**. Primary archive for modern openings, names and mileage. An archive index is a research route, not proof of an individual date.
- [MTR investor presentation, January 2018][p-mtr-island-west] — **New**. Slide 35: West Island Line 28 December 2014, Sai Ying Pun 29 March 2015, Kwun Tong extension 23 October 2016 and South Island Line 28 December 2016.
- [MTR PR030/22: East Rail cross-harbour opening][p-mtr-erl-2022] — **New**. Passenger service from 15 May 2022, Hung Hom–Admiralty and Exhibition Centre station.
- [EMSD: Tuen Ma Line Phase 1 opening][p-mtr-tml-2020] — **New**. 14 February 2020 and the distinction between Phase 1 and the later full line.

### Historical coverage and outstanding evidence

- Sha Tau Kok is split at its public openings: Fanling–Shek Chung Au on 1911-12-21,
  then Sha Tau Kok on 1912-04-01; both close on 1928-04-01. The opening notices are
  transcribed in the [branch history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sha_Tau_Kok_Branch).
  [KCRC](https://www.kcrc.com/en/about-kcrc/history.html) gives the full route as 11.6 km.
  The map includes Fanling, Hung Leng, Wo Hang, Shek Chung Au and Sha Tau Kok.
  Lung Yeuk Tau's location/closure and the five February 1916 halts (Kwan Tei, Ma Mei Ha,
  Loi Tung, Tai Long, San Tsuen) remain unresolved; do not invent exact days or positions.
- Che Kung Miu is a separate historical halt, not the present Che Kung Temple station.
  KCR's [1935 report](https://www.histsyn.com/2023/01/AR1935.html), paragraphs 59 and 102,
  records its opening on November 16 near Bridge 12; the
  [1936 report](https://www.histsyn.com/2023/01/AR1936.html), paragraph 41, records closure
  on October 1. Historical geometry follows the existing map's approximate scale.
- The original Kowloon terminus and Chatham Road approach are separate from East Tsim Sha Tsui's
  2004 tunnel. The [1975 replacement](https://www.histsyn.com/2023/01/kcr1976.html) and
  [1981 Beacon Hill Tunnel switchover](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beacon_Hill_Tunnel_(Hong_Kong)>)
  retain the modern track geometry. Short switchover gaps are collapsed under §7.
- High Speed Rail's Hong Kong section opens on 2018-09-23, per
  [MTR's 2018 report](https://www.mtr.com.hk/archive/corporate/en/investor/annual2018/E110.pdf).
  Its 25.7 km value uses [MTR's business overview](https://www.mtr.com.hk/archive/corporate/en/publications/images/business_overview_e.pdf)
  rather than the rounded 26 km project length. Its curve follows the
  [published alignment](https://www.legco.gov.hk/yr16-17/english/panels/tp/tp_rdp/papers/tp_rdp20161209cb4-243-9-e.pdf)
  through Shek Kong and Mai Po, continuing towards Futian and off the map's northern edge.
  The Shenzhen continuation supplies geographic context from the Hong Kong opening date;
  the kilometres and station count cover only the Hong Kong section. No boundary station is added.
- This is **not yet a complete historical inventory**. KCRC records a Sheung Shui halt in 1913;
  the map still starts at the dated 1930 station opening. KCR's
  [1921 report](https://www.histsyn.com/2022/12/AR1921.html), paragraph 19, also records a
  Ho Mun Tin halt without an exact opening day. Both need dated timetables and location evidence.
  The old Hung Hom closure (June 13 versus September 15/16, 1921) and the precise 1996 renaming
  date remain disputed; the existing dates are retained, not newly certified.
- Light Rail tracks now distinguish the 1988-09-14–16 free-ride preview, the 1988-09-18 opening, 1988-09-24 northern/estate
  branches, 1991-11-03 southern extension, 1992-02-02 eastern/Sam Shing extensions,
  1993-01-10 Tin Shui branch, 1995-03-26 Tin Shui Wai Terminus extension, and 2003-12-07
  northern/eastern Tin Shui Wai extensions. Existing modern curves and stroke widths are retained.
  The [contemporary opening notice](https://att.hkitalk.net/HKiTalk2/data/attachment/forum/202303/04/105705khyhdansbyz8h0gs.jpeg)
  lists free public rides on routes 610/611/612 on September 14–16, no service on the 17th, and
  fare-paying service from September 18. Under §7 the line is drawn from September 14 and stays through the
  September 18 opening (the no-service day is not drawn as a closure); both dates have events. Routes 505/506 and the
  "whole network except 507 and 512" date of September 25 in the same notice are not yet
  reconciled with the 1988-09-24 branch date. Route 506's September 23 introduction uses
  existing track; its individual stops are outside this map's Light Rail scope.
  The [government's November 6, 1991 bulletin](https://www.histsyn.com/2022/12/daily-information-bulletin-1990s-1991_13.html)
  says the southern extension opened the previous Sunday (November 3), consistent with the
  November 4 newspaper cited by [Goodview Garden's history](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/豐景園站).
  This takes precedence over the November 17 date in several English station articles.
  The [stop chronology](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_Rail_(MTR)#Stops>) identifies the 1992,
  1993 and 1995 stages; [LegCo's commissioning report](https://www.legco.gov.hk/yr03-04/english/panels/tp/tp_rdp/papers/tp_rdp1219cb1-613-1e.pdf)
  confirms December 7, 2003. Tin Shui's former terminus position is interpolated on the existing
  curve; stop-scale turning loops and the 2002–03 grade-separation realignments remain simplified.
  Stage kilometres are the estimates described under the SVG notes below.
- Existing route kilometres are estimates: distinguish route length, construction length
  and the operator's exclusion of duplicated sections before recalibrating individual paths.

### SVG geography, identities and measurement limits

The original SVG carried the title “MTR system map in English released to the public domain” (removed in the September 2026 normalisation, since spec §3 bans `<title>`); its exact upstream Commons revision has not been recovered. Do not treat that embedded statement as full provenance for later additions. The background geography was replaced on 23 September 2026 using the sources below; the KCR/Sha Tau Kok reconstructions still require historical maps rather than modern track data.

- Coastlines and islands: © [OpenStreetMap contributors](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright), data under [ODbL 1.0](https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/odbl/1-0/), from [Geofabrik's Guangdong extract, including Hong Kong and Macau](https://download.geofabrik.de/asia/china/guangdong.html), snapshot `guangdong-260923.osm.pbf` (data through `2026-09-23T20:22:04Z`). Uses the mapped `natural=coastline` ways, including airport reclamation, harbour quays, Deep Bay and outlying islands; small offshore polygons below 0.5 SVG square units are omitted for legibility.
- Hong Kong/Shenzhen land colours: [Hong Kong administrative boundary, OSM relation 913110](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/913110). The visible border river uses the mapped water polygon [relation 9791660](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/9791660), rather than an invented gap between the land shapes. Its upper reach along the border ([way 536414810](https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/536414810)) and the Sha Tau Kok River ([way 509324162](https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/509324162), up to the Chung Ying Street culvert) are drawn from their mapped banks (2026-10-02); before, both stopped as hairlines at the original artwork's edge. A thin cover in the matching colours hides the anti-aliasing seams along the four edges of that artwork's clip rectangle. The relation's Huanggang Port Hong Kong Port Area rings, north of the river at Huanggang, are left out as too small to read; that area is drawn as Shenzhen land (2026-10-02). Reservoirs above the overview threshold are drawn throughout: inside the original artwork's bounds the inland-water layer is hidden by the original land fills, so Plover Cove, Shek Pik and (since 2026-10-03) [Tai Lam Chung](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/1295878) are redrawn on top of it.
- Registration: WGS84 coordinates fitted to the existing map using modern East Rail, Tsuen Wan, Tung Chung and Tuen Ma station control points. Coastlines were simplified with a topology-preserving tolerance of 0.25 SVG units, without moving railway paths or stations. This improves the background's geographic accuracy within the original map's approximate projection; it is not a survey. The background shows **present-day geography throughout playback**, not historical reclamation stages.

- Sha Tau Kok and early KCR: museum booklet and annual reports above. Historic curves and station positions remain approximate; a date citation does not certify their coordinates.
- Modern geographic cross-checks: [East Rail](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/4248589), [Tsuen Wan](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/269669), [Tung Chung](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/5317704), [Tuen Ma](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/6102298), [XRL](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/9405634).
- The XRL geometry was corrected through Kwai Chung/Shek Kong using mapped track plus the LegCo alignment. It continues into Shenzhen at the SVG boundary; only Hong Kong mileage is counted. Old Beacon Hill and Tsim Sha Tsui approaches are historical reconstructions, not current OSM railway.
- Light Rail is simplified. The documented allocation is 36.2 km today, with 4.4 km for 2003 extensions, 3.2 km for earlier Tin Shui Wai track and 28.6 km for the older Tuen Mun/Yuen Long area. Splits within that last group were prorated by drawn length: **estimates, not measured historical engineering lengths**.
- Airport Express and the Tung Chung line share one pair of tracks west of Tsing Yi, across the Tsing Ma Bridge to Lantau; Airport Express passes through Sunny Bay on the centre tracks ([Tung Chung line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tung_Chung_line), [Sunny Bay station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Bay_station)). The map draws the two lines side by side instead of the dashed Airport Express overlay on the Tung Chung centreline it used on Lantau and from Kowloon to Hong Kong. On the shared track they touch (`0.95 W`, like Shanghai's Lines 3/4), with Airport Express on the north side on Lantau; they part to `2 W` round Sunny Bay and from Tsing Yi to Hong Kong, where Tung Chung-only stations need the clearance. Airport Express crosses to the south side just after Sunny Bay, where the tracks really divide (it runs through the station's centre tracks), and west of Siu Ho Wan it follows its real alignment, crossing the Tung Chung line on its loop past Tung Chung towards the airport (moved up to 8.4 units on 2026-10-01). On the shared track neither line has a real side, and this one swap avoids crossings with the Disneyland Resort, Tsuen Wan or Tuen Ma lines that would read as interchanges. Its 34.0 km Hong Kong - Airport track and the 1.3 km AsiaWorld-Expo extension give the published 35.3 km.
- Termini end at their station markers. Tails that continued past a terminus were trimmed: Tsuen Wan, Kennedy Town, North Point (Kwun Tong and Tseung Kwan O lines), Tiu Keng Leng, Lok Ma Chau, Wu Kai Sha, LOHAS Park, Chai Wan, Whampoa, Sunny Bay, AsiaWorld-Expo, the 1979–80 Tsim Sha Tsui terminus and the Tung Chung line at both ends. Light Rail branch ends now finish on the centreline of the track they join, so their caps stay inside it. Every track end at a station lies on that line's platform point (see Station markers and accuracy pass, 2026-10-01). The KCR line always ends at Lo Wu (moved about 4 units west-northwest onto its OSM position on 2026-09-29). From 1911-10-05 to 1949-10-14 trains ran on into China and Lo Wu had no station, so the 1910–1975 track's Lo Wu end is marked `data-continues` and that track has a round cap (spec §4); the later tracks end inside the Lo Wu marker and have neither; no stub is drawn on to the boundary, because a few hundred metres of track could not show that the service ran through to Canton. Kai Tak (terminus 2020-02-14 to 2021-06-27) moved 2.8 units along the line towards its OSM position (from 117 m off to about 50 m), and the two Tuen Ma tracks meet at its centre; on 2026-10-03 it moved a further 0.87 onto its OSM platform, with the joint.
- Stations and tracks were checked against OpenStreetMap on 2026-09-29 (platform stop positions from the route relations, converted to map units with local fits on neighbouring stations; on Lantau, with a fit of OSM's Airport Express and Tung Chung tracks to the drawn ones). Markers more than 1.5 W off were moved onto their platforms and the approaching tracks redrawn along the mapped track: the Tseung Kwan O Line north of Tseung Kwan O and the LOHAS Park branch; East Rail from University to Tai Wai, with the Racecourse spur 3.4 units east of the main line rejoining it at Fo Tan; East Rail from Sha Tin and the Ma On Shan/Tuen Ma approaches into Tai Wai (Tai Wai moved about 7 units north-east; [the station's history](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/大圍站) puts the 1986 station on the present site, expanded in place in 2004; the 1983–86 temporary station, north of it near today's Tai Wai industrial area, and the 1935–36 Che Kung Miu halt keep their approximate positions on the redrawn track); the whole Ma On Shan line; the Tsuen Wan line from Kwai Fong to Prince Edward and from Tsim Sha Tsui to Central (the 1980–82 Modified Initial System track follows it); the Kwun Tong line through Diamond Hill and Choi Hung and the Whampoa extension; the Island Line through Fortress Hill; the Tseung Kwan O Line from Quarry Bay to North Point (and the 2001–02 Kwun Tong track); the 2009 West Rail extension from Hung Hom to Nam Cheong and the 2004–09 East Rail track to East Tsim Sha Tsui; Tuen Ma around Mei Foo and Ho Man Tin; East Rail into Hung Hom and the 2022 cross-harbour section; the whole South Island Line; the Disneyland Resort line; and the Lok Ma Chau spur's station end. Interchange markers were rebuilt from the lines' platform points (2026-10-01 bullet), their earlier single-line circles with them. Where two lines share a corridor they are drawn side by side at 1 W (since 2026-10-03 exactly touching; see the final audit bullet), the Tuen Ma line crossing East Rail north of Hung Hom and running 1 W west of it into the station. Mei Foo is drawn as two dots on the two separate platform groups (about 260 m apart), joined by a bridge. Termini moved with their tracks: Po Lam, LOHAS Park, Wu Kai Sha, Tuen Mun (West Rail trimmed back to the platform), Tung Chung, Airport, AsiaWorld-Expo, Hong Kong, Hong Kong West Kowloon, Lok Ma Chau, Lo Wu and both Ngong Ping 360 terminals. Other stations were slid along their own tracks. The Beacon Hill tunnel tracks keep their own alignments south of Hin Keng. The Island Line's 1985 and 1986 tracks meet at Admiralty's Island Line platform point (the 1985–86 terminus). Kilometre values were not changed. South of Hung Hom the East Rail stays 1 W east of the Tuen Ma line until they part. (The West Kowloon High Speed Rail approach was redrawn on 2026-10-03; see the final audit bullet.)
- Station markers and accuracy pass (2026-10-01). Each interchange is drawn from one platform point per line: the OSM platform centre (platform ways next to the line's route-relation stop positions, else the stop positions) projected with a local 10-station fit onto that line's drawn track. Which platforms form one shape is set out in the interchange shapes bullet below. Bridges are straight where the walk stays within 1 W of the line. Earlier single-line circles sit on their line's dot. Tracks redrawn along OSM: West Rail Kam Sheung Road–Tuen Mun (up to 2.2 W), East Rail Sheung Shui–Tai Po and the Lok Ma Chau spur (1.7–1.9 W), Tseung Kwan O Line into Tiu Keng Leng (1.3 W, now 1 W beside the Kwun Tong Line), the 1981 Beacon Hill tunnel beside Tuen Ma past Hin Keng, and the Kwun Tong Line at Lok Fu; the 1910–1983 Tai Po Market circle moved 2.3 units to the railway museum. Every track end at a station lies on its line's platform point (the Admiralty 1985–86 Island Line terminus and the joints at Argyle, Yau Tong, Quarry Bay and Central). Dates, labels and kilometres are unchanged.
- Final audit (2026-10-01): Tsim Sha Tsui's circle moved 0.48 units onto the Tsuen Wan line, with the 1979–82 Modified Initial System tracks run along it there (the same tunnel) and the East Tsim Sha Tsui connector following. Admiralty is composed as the real station: the Tsuen Wan/Island cross-platform pair is one blob, chained by bridges to the South Island dot and on to the East Rail dot (one dot radius back along its track, their OSM platform centres lying end to end), so East Rail visibly ends in its own dot. The 1910 KCR track, which held two pieces either side of the Beacon Hill tunnel, is split into Lo Wu – Tai Wai (26.0 km) and Kowloon Tong – Mong Kok East (2.9 km), totalling the former 28.9 km; the Beacon Hill tracks meet them at the Tai Wai and Kowloon Tong platforms. A hairpin control point at the start of the 2003 West Rail track at Nam Cheong was removed.
- Smoothness pass (2026-10-01): every track is tangent-continuous except the Ngong Ping 360 cable, whose two corners are its real angle stations. The Tseung Kwan O Line's 2002 start at Yau Tong and the Kwun Tong Line's 2001 start at Quarry Bay had short backward stubs left by end trims; they now leave their platform points along the line (changes of 0.02 units), and a 20° corner in the 1979 Modified Initial System track south of Waterloo is rounded (0.15 units). East Rail crosses the Tsuen Wan line once north-east of Admiralty, where the real tracks cross, and then ends at its own platform beside it inside the station marker.
- Interchange shapes (2026-10-01), spec §5 rule 2 (Hong Kong's route map draws every interchange as one capsule, so it carries no composition): one shape only where the lines share track or their platforms cross in plan one over the other. Full stacked crossings, one circle on the drawn crossing: Ho Man Tin (cruciform station, Tuen Ma L5 crossing over Kwun Tong L7) and Quarry Bay (OpenStreetMap footprints of the Island line platforms, layer −3, cross over the deep Kwun Tong/Tseung Kwan O platforms, layer −5, at about 40°; the transfer is still a long passage and two escalator flights). No Hong Kong interchange shares track. Every other interchange is separate dots at the real platforms joined by a bridge, overlapping where close: cross-platform pairs on their own tracks (Prince Edward, Mong Kok, Yau Tong, Tiu Keng Leng, Lai King, North Point, Admiralty's Island/Tsuen Wan pair), lines on separate levels running parallel (Yau Ma Tei; Admiralty's East Rail over the South Island line; Hung Hom; Diamond Hill), side-by-side platforms (Tai Wai, Nam Cheong, Sunny Bay, Tsing Yi, Kowloon, Hong Kong, Fanling's Sha Tau Kok bay), Light Rail stops beside or below the Tuen Ma stations (Yuen Long, Siu Hong, Tuen Mun, Tin Shui Wai), and passages (Kowloon Tong, Mei Foo, Central).
- Close platforms (2026-10-02, spec §5 rule 3): separate shapes closer than 0.4 R read as one lump even fully zoomed in, so they are drawn as one shape through the same platform points, which do not move: Admiralty (East Rail and South Island, 0.21 R). Pairs 0.4 R or more apart stay separate dots.
- Track segments (2026-10-02, spec §4 one growth per event): the KCR British Section opening of 1910-10-01 (four pieces) grows as one path from Kowloon to Lo Wu. On 1975-11-30 the Chatham Road–Kowloon stretch retracts and the rest is handed over in place, and on 1981-04-26 the old Beacon Hill tunnel retracts and Kowloon Tong–Mong Kok East and Tai Wai–Lo Wu are handed over in place, so nothing regrows. 10 other single-piece openings now grow from the end that meets the network already open. Geometry, km and colours are unchanged; this was checked by km per line on every date and by a tracks-only pixel comparison on every change date and the day before.
- Final audit (2026-10-03). Markers are dots at the real platforms, so tracks follow their real courses and neighbouring lines either touch exactly or keep the standard 2 W spacing. Corridors were rebuilt from OpenStreetMap (active-contour fit of each line's mapped tracks through the local 10-station fit): where two lines' real tracks are closer than 1 W (within 0.6 units of it) they are drawn exactly 1 W apart (stroke gap 0, fitted to within 0.003), and where the real tracks part the gap opens along the real curves. Fixed this way: the Tsuen Wan and Kwun Tong lines from Prince Edward to the Kwun Tong split south of Yau Ma Tei (the Tsuen Wan line had run 1.3-2.5 units west of its course, leaving a 0.78 W sliver; it moved about 1.1 units east; Prince Edward, Mong Kok and Yau Ma Tei dots followed, and the 1979-82 Argyle and Waterloo circles now sit on the Kwun Tong dots); East Rail and Tuen Ma from Tai Wai to Hin Keng (a 0.03-0.14 hairline gap over 10 units); the Tsuen Wan and Tung Chung lines at Lai King; the Tuen Ma and Tung Chung lines from Mei Foo to West Kowloon; the Tuen Ma and Kwun Tong lines into Diamond Hill (the Tuen Ma line now crosses the Kwun Tong line at a clear angle west of the station); the Kwun Tong and Tseung Kwan O lines from Yau Tong to Tiu Keng Leng (gap varied 0.08-1.66); the Tsuen Wan and Island lines west of Admiralty (overlapped by up to 0.5); the Disneyland Resort and Tung Chung lines at Sunny Bay (overlapped by 0.05); and East Rail with the Tuen Ma line through Hung Hom (overlapped by up to 0.3; their real tracks are stacked and cross under the station, so the Tuen Ma line crosses East Rail north of it on a short transition and leaves south-west along its real curve). The 2 W widenings at Olympic and Hin Keng were dropped: the real tracks are together there, the widening bent both lines off their courses, and each dot stays on its platform beside the passing line (spec section 5). North of North Point the Tseung Kwan O line (and the 2001-02 Kwun Tong track on the same course) was widened from a 0.77 W gap to the standard 2 W beside the Island Line (moved up to 0.4). Single-line stretches redrawn along OSM: East Rail from Kowloon Tong through Mong Kok East to Hung Hom and under the harbour (the visible corner at the 1975 Hung Hom approach joint is now a smooth curve; Mong Kok East moved 1.41 onto its platform; the 1910 and 1975 tracks share the new section exactly and the 1910 Chatham Road approach meets the projected joint), the Kwun Tong Whampoa extension (up to 1.75 off) with Ho Man Tin on the new drawn crossing, the Tsuen Wan line Sham Shui Po - Prince Edward and Yau Ma Tei - Tsim Sha Tsui (Jordan 0.44 onto its platform), the Tuen Ma line Diamond Hill - Kai Tak - To Kwa Wan (Kai Tak 0.87, To Kwa Wan 0.77) and Mei Foo - Tsuen Wan West, the Kwun Tong line Choi Hung - Kwun Tong - Lam Tin - Yau Tong (Kowloon Bay 0.78, Ngau Tau Kok 0.40), the Tseung Kwan O line Tiu Keng Leng - Hang Hau (Tseung Kwan O 0.72), the Island Line Admiralty - North Point, Quarry Bay - Chai Wan and Sheung Wan - Kennedy Town (Tai Koo 0.91, Sai Wan Ho 1.32, Shau Kei Wan 1.04; Central's Island Line dot 0.96), and the whole Disneyland Resort line. The High Speed Rail follows its tunnel (OSM ways [331353198](https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/331353198) and [627724824](https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/627724824)) near Nam Cheong and into West Kowloon, touching the Tuen Ma line where the real tunnels run together and crossed by it as it leaves for Austin (it had run 1 W west of the tunnel, overlapping the Tung Chung line). The 1979-82 Modified Initial System and 1980-82 Tsim Sha Tsui - Chater tracks share the present Kwun Tong and Tsuen Wan courses exactly, with a smooth crossover south of Waterloo; the 2004-09 East Tsim Sha Tsui branch takes the Tuen Ma course (the same tunnel); the 1989-2002 and 2001-02 Kwun Tong tracks follow the Eastern Harbour Crossing course the Tseung Kwan O line uses (they had been drawn up to 1 unit off, with a hairpin south of Lam Tin), and Quarry Bay 1989-2002 is one circle on the drawn crossing like its successor. Every joint between consecutive tracks of a line is exactly coincident and tangent (Kwun Tong, Yau Tong, Admiralty and Hung Hom had 0.1-1.2 degree kinks). Every station dot was re-projected from its OSM platform onto its corrected track; all present-day dots now lie within 0.75 units (along the track) of their platform centres, except Quarry Bay, which sits on its drawn crossing (spec section 5 rule 2b); the old Tai Po Market, temporary Tai Wai and temporary Hung Hom circles keep their historical positions. No interchange shapes are closer than 0.4 R (cross-platform pairs are 0.65 R apart). Route kilometres are unchanged. The joint seams that Chromium draws where two exactly aligned, tangent tracks meet (e.g. at the 1975 Hung Hom approach joint) are a renderer artefact. Left as drawn: Light Rail (simplified); the Tung Chung / Airport Express pair, whose documented convention (Airport Express touching on Lantau, 2 W from Tsing Yi) leaves the Tung Chung line up to 1.6 W off its course between stations on Lantau and east of Tsing Yi (the 10-station fit is weak on Lantau, where the earlier pass fitted OSM to the drawn tracks); the real double crossing of East Rail under the Tsuen Wan line north-east of Admiralty (the lens between them is hidden under the Tsuen Wan line); AsiaWorld-Expo, whose dot sits on the drawn coastline (the network and coastline fits differ by about 1 unit at the airport island's north-east corner). Events were re-checked through 2026-10-02: no MTR line, station or rename opened after 15 May 2022 (Kwu Tung is expected in 2027, Tung Chung East and West in 2029, Oyster Bay in 2030 and the Northern Link in 2034; [Kwu Tung station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwu_Tung_station), [MTR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTR)).

<a id="shanghai"></a>

## Shanghai (`shanghai`)

Assets: [events](../src/assets/shanghai/data/events.json), [line names](../src/assets/shanghai/data/lines.json), [SVG](../src/assets/shanghai/map.svg).

Scope: Shanghai Metro, the Shanghai Suburban Railway lines (Jinshan Railway, Airport Link Line) and the Maglev, with the Songjiang trams as tracks only. Station tooltips use `metro`, `suburban` (Jinshan Railway and Airport Link stations) and `maglev`. Maglev stations show Shanghai Maglev Transportation's swoosh (`shanghai-maglev.svg`), cropped from the [public-domain SMT logo](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:SMT_logo.svg) with its "SMT" lettering removed and the viewBox padded top and bottom so the wide swoosh matches the other logos' visual weight at tooltip height. Pudong Airport shows only the Maglev symbol until Line 2 arrives on 2010-04-08. The first public days of Line 1 are an open question under the spec §7 opening rule (accuracy gap 2 and the 1993-05-28 row). The Maglev appears on 2003-01-01 with weekend sightseeing round trips and stays on the map through the 2003-03-10 – 2003-09-19 pause (software upgrade, then SARS; spec §7 draws no gap), and its airport opening (2003-10-11), daily trial operation (2003-12-29) and commercial operation (2006-04-27) are separate events.

### Primary records and other focused references

- [Timeline of Shanghai Metro][p-sh-timeline] — **Recovered**. User-specified completeness checklist; secondary, not final authority where dates conflict. Includes renames, transfers and temporary closures beyond this build-history scope.
- [Minhang government account: thirty years of Shanghai Metro][p-sh-early] — **New**. Line 1 historical opening stages; government-authored retrospective hosted by The Paper.
- [Shanghai government: South Railway Station and Xinzhuang opening][p-sh-xinzhuang] — **New**. Xinzhuang's first Jinshan Railway passenger train on 5 January 2025; do not confuse the mainline high-speed upgrade with a new metro line.
- [Shanghai government / Jinshan district: 1·5 timetable change][p-sh-jinshan-timetable] — **New**. Dated timetable and fare-map images for Jinshan services from 5 January 2025.
- [Shanghai Basic Facts 2024][p-sh-statistics] — **New**. Government network statistics and geographic context; aggregate length only, not a source for each SVG segment.
- [Shanghai Release: Jinghong Road temporary underground passage][p-sh-jinghong-open] — **New**. Operator announcement reproduced by Shanghai Release/Sina: 5 July 2025 opening and unchanged fare system.

| 1993-05-28 | Line 1: Xujiahui - Jinjiang Park opens                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | [Minhang government account: thirty years of Shanghai Metro][p-sh-early]; [上海轨道交通1号线][sh-1-zh]; [Timeline of Shanghai Metro][sh-timeline]; Recovered citation: [Shanghai government local-history archive: urban transport / infrastructure][r-sh-1993-05-28]. **Note:** Early stations and the original Jinjiang Park alignment require the historical station chronology, not today’s Line 1 station list. **Note (spec §7):** 28 May 1993 is the double-track trial operation in the Xuhui district account ([The Paper, 28 May 2023](https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_23259606)) and the municipal chronicle text reproduced by [chinametro.net](https://web.archive.org/web/2023/http://chinametro.net/index.php?aid=32452&id=425&m=newscon) ("5月28日，南段双线开通试运营"). An earlier one-train, single-track sightseeing service on Xujiahui – Jinjiang Park, sold with 5-yuan 观光票, began on 28 January 1993 according to [Xinmin Weekly](https://paper.xinmin.cn/html/xmzk/2022-03-14/20/27558.html) ("1993年1月28日，一号线南段（徐家汇站—锦江乐园站）6.6公里率先试通车，作为观光段来试运营…5元一张的观光票"; also [Xinmin Weekly 6679](https://m.xinminweekly.com.cn/content/6679.html)), and before the Spring Festival (23 January) according to the chief commander's [oral history](https://news.qq.com/rain/a/20230526A05CJ900) and [The Paper, "上海1993"](https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_21627405); the Minhang account in The Paper gives 9 April ("4月9日…开通，对外售票观光试运营"). Sightseeing counts under §7, but the first day is disputed and nothing says whether rides ran continuously from January to May, so the recorded date stays (accuracy gap 2). |

neither is a contemporary source and continuity to April is unknown, so the recorded date stays (accuracy gap 2).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

| 1999-09-20 | Line 2: People's Park opens as a separate station from Line 1's People's Square; Line 2: Zhongshan Park - Longyang Road service for organised visitor groups begins                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | [上海轨道交通1号线][sh-1-zh]; [上海轨道交通2号线][sh-2-zh]; [Timeline of Shanghai Metro][sh-timeline]; Recovered citation: [Shanghai government local-history archive: urban transport / infrastructure][r-sh-1999-09-20]; [China News Service, 20 September 1999](https://web.archive.org/web/20200201082312/http://finance.sina.com.cn/news/1999-9-21/7044.html) "先行组织社会各方和地铁建设者观光". **Note (spec §7):** the 试通车 (trial running, on the up track according to the [1999 yearbook][r-sh-1999-09-20]) first carried organised visitor groups; the same report expected public 5-yuan sightseeing tickets from mid/late October (en.wikipedia gives 28 October from a SHINE infographic). Both are passenger service under §7, so the line opens on 20 September. Regular fares and a 16h40 daily timetable began on 11 June 2000 ([Xinbao via Sina](https://web.archive.org/web/20180328231226/http://news.sina.com.cn/china/2000-06-11/96584.html) "在试通车运行近9个月后，今天中午12时正式通车"), recorded as its own event.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

| 2003-01-01 | Maglev: Longyang Road - Pudong International Airport weekend and holiday sightseeing round trips begin, without alighting at the airport                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | [Xinwen Chenbao via Sina, 2 January 2003](http://news.sina.com.cn/c/2003-01-02/0205859648.shtml) "上海磁浮列车昨日首次开放…昨日共有1200位市民有幸乘上磁浮…从现在起到春节前的双休日，以及2月1-7日…都将向普通市民开放"; [Eastday via Sina, 1 January 2003](http://news.sina.com.cn/c/2003-01-01/0122858988.shtml) "每逢双休日及国家法定假日…普通舱150元，贵宾舱为300元(龙阳路站到浦东国际机场站来回)"; [People's Daily East China edition via Sina, 10 February 2003](http://news.sina.com.cn/c/2003-02-10/0211901881.shtml) (18,000 riders over the Spring Festival). **Note (spec §7):** paid public sightseeing round trips on weekends and holidays count; riders did not alight at the airport, but the train ran the whole line, so both stations are drawn. The 31 December 2002 inaugural ride was a VIP ride.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
